decisions.reason: The complete published Hackl2009 body now removes the former local-text gap. Its own SPC experiments empirically show quantifier-dependent intermediate processing profiles for truth-conditionally equivalent most/more-than-half judgments on the same arrays, despite nonsignificant overall accuracy/RT. The current within-subject Most1/Most2 comparison on identical two-color displays also holds truth conditions constant and tests whether lexical quantifier semantics forces different verification profiles; the conclusion expressly confirms and extends Hackl. It is a conceptual retest of this lexical computational nonequivalence component, not a claimed reproduction of the original particular lead-counting versus half-criterion algorithm or incremental timing statistic. Changed quantifiers, flash presentation and performance measure do not alone exclude that test. Lidz2011 explicitly discusses Hackl but its own experiment varies color diversity for most alone: it is the closest subtraction/color-invariance comparison, already row2248, rather than an intervening experiment comparing two lexical quantifiers. Thus Hackl adds an independently attributed original-specific comparison absent from the represented Lidz row. Current true/false directional reversal, nonsignificant language-specific RTs and formula/prose inconsistency remain; no outcome, participant independence, or identical algorithm is inferred.

I tested the processing of two majority quantifiers in Bulgarian (Bg) and Polish (Pl): the
counterpart of English most (povečeto in Bg, większość in Pl, henceforth Most1) and a closely
related quantifier with the meaning of “the largest subset” (naj-mnogo in Bg, najwięcej in Pl,
henceforth Most2). I obtained three notable results:
• Most1 is verified by a Subtraction strategy as in (2) and not (3), directly replicating the
findings of Lidz et al. for Slavic;
• Most2 is verified by a Selection strategy as in (4) in accordance with its lexical semantics;
• the canonical verification strategies are used even in cases where either strategy would yield
the correct truth value.

decisions.reason: Throughout the paper (lines 4-7, 25-26, 36-43, 131-132), Tomaszewicz (2012) explicitly identifies Lidz, Pietroski, Hunter, and Halberda (2011) (already represented by shipped row 2248, 10.1007/s11050-010-9062-6, and coded at target_index 2) as the closest antecedent in the Pietroski/Lidz/Hunter/Halberda dot-verification research chain whose Subtraction verification finding for 'most' ((2) vs. (3)) is directly replicated for Slavic Most1. While the concluding sentence (lines 185-186) provides affirmative contrary context by stating that the results 'confirm and extend the findings of Pietroski et al. (2008), Hackl (2009), Lidz et al. (2011),' and shared authorship does not make Pietroski et al. (2008) an equivalent report to Lidz et al. (2011), the current text never specifies a separate empirical finding or contrast from Pietroski et al. (2008) distinct from the Lidz et al. (2011) subtraction/dot-verification chain already captured by shipped row 2248. Under the codebook replication-chain rule, only the closest antecedent in that chain (Lidz et al. 2011) is coded.
